caption:
Shopping for a W463 G 500? The year matters more than the mileage.

2002–04: early US trucks have the electrical gremlins. Seat motors, window regulators, door-lock and transfer-case actuators.
2005–08: the sweet spot. Specialists say the faults were mostly gone by 2005–06.

And mind the gearbox: the seven-speed 7G-Tronic arrived with June 2006 production, the 2007 model year in the US. 2005–06 trucks keep the simpler five-speed. How to tell which one you're looking at is in our G 500 guide at boxytrucks.com.

Whatever the year, check for rust where nobody cleans: the tailgate's lower edge, door bottoms, sills and the rear frame tubes.

Mine's a 2007, the first US year with the 7-speed.

caption:
Land Cruiser 80 Series buying guide: 5 things to check before you hand over the money.

1. Pull the front knuckle fill plug. Runny grease means diff oil is getting in and the inner axle seals have gone.
2. Look for coolant weeping at the head-to-block joint.
3. Get underneath: rust in the front footwells and around the rear windows.
4. Look for cracks in the frame around the steering box, especially on trucks that have run 33s.
5. Run every window and engage every locker. On my 80 it was the regulators and a vacuum leak at the lockers. – Hank

title: G-Wagen W463: 5 things to check
caption:
G-Wagen W463 buying guide: 5 things to check before you buy one.

1. Rust where nobody cleans: around the sunroof, under the tail-lights, the door hinges, the rear spring perches and the windscreen seal.
2. Engage all three lockers, centre, rear, then front, on loose ground. Lockers that were never used often don't work.
3. Hold it at 55–70 mph. Judder can mean a failing propshaft; harsh 2–3 shifts point to old fluid or the conductor plate.
4. Know the year: 2002–04 US trucks have the electrical gremlins. Much better by 2005–06.
5. Look underneath for oil. On my 2007 G500, the oil filter housing gasket leak was my biggest issue. – Hank

All 8 checks, the years to avoid and a free printable checklist: boxytrucks.com (link in bio). Save this for your next test drive.

title: Defender 90/110: 5 things to check
caption:
Land Rover Defender 90 / 110 buying guide: 5 things to check first.

1. Paperwork: the VIN plate on the brake servo should match the number on the front chassis rail, and an import must really be 25+ years old.
2. The rear crossmember rots from the inside. Fresh underseal or checker plate can hide it.
3. Bulkhead: footwells, bottom corners and under the vent flaps. A new one runs about £1,600 in the UK.
4. Swivel balls: pitted chrome chews the seals and wears the pins. Wobbly steering points here.
5. Is it really a NAS? Real 1993 NAS 110s and 1994–97 NAS 90s have numbered badges and US VINs.

title: 4th Gen 4Runner: 5 things to check
caption:
4th Gen 4Runner (2003–09) buying guide: 5 things to check first.

1. Frame: salt-belt trucks rot. Take a hammer and a light to the rails, crossmembers and rear link mounts.
2. V8 secondary air injection: it can fail around 100–150k miles, with a check-engine light, limp mode and a $2,000–4,000 bill.
3. V8 timing belt: the V8 has a belt (the V6 a chain), due at 90,000 miles or nine years. Ask for the receipt.
4. V6 coolant loss: 2003–05 head gaskets. A cylinder 6 misfire (P0306) plus coolant loss is the red flag.
5. X-REAS and rear air: leaky X-REAS shocks get replaced in pairs, and on Limiteds the rear shouldn't sag overnight.

All 8 checks, the years to avoid and a free printable checklist: boxytrucks.com (link in bio). Save this for your next test drive.

caption:
Land Rover Series IIA: how to tell an early one from a late one in five seconds.

I spotted these two Series IIA Station Wagons this summer.

Early IIA (1961–69): the headlamps sit inboard, in the grille panel. The green one is a short-wheelbase 88.
Late IIA (1969–71): the headlamps moved out into the wings, and the grille is still metal. The Series III got a plastic one.
88 or 109? The long-wheelbase 109 Station Wagon adds a row of side windows behind the doors.
